summary.text: Factor the odd composite modulus as \(m=pv\), with \(p\) prime and either \(p\mid v\) or \((p,v)=1\); in the first case the unit \(1+v\) has \(v^2=0\pmod m\), so \((1+v)^n=1+nv\), and the required \(\pm1\) alternative forces \(p\mid n\), contradicting \(p\mid 2n+1\). In the coprime case, an assumed base with \(b^n=-1\pmod m\) yields via the Chinese remainder theorem a unit congruent to \(1\pmod p\) and \(b\pmod v\), whose \(n\)-th power is \((1,-1)\), neither globally \(1\) nor \(-1\) because both factors are odd and greater than one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
m=2n+1.
\]
Recall that
\[
a(n)=\#\{b\in\{1,2,\ldots,m-1\}:b^n\equiv-1\pmod m\}.
\]
Suppose that \(m\) is an absolute Euler pseudoprime. Thus \(m>1\), \(m\) is composite, and for every integer \(c\) coprime to \(m\),
\[
c^{(m-1)/2}\equiv 1\pmod m
\quad\text{or}\quad
c^{(m-1)/2}\equiv-1\pmod m.
\]
Since \(m=2n+1\), we have \((m-1)/2=n\). Consequently, the defining property may be written as
\[
\gcd(c,m)=1\implies c^n\equiv\pm1\pmod m. \tag{1}
\]
We shall prove that no \(b\) in the range \(1\le b<m\) can satisfy \(b^n\equiv-1\pmod m\).

We first record the factorization reduction that will be used. Because \(m>1\) is composite, it has a prime divisor \(p\), and we may write
\[
m=pv
\]
with \(v>1\). Indeed, if the complementary factor were \(1\), then \(m=p\) would itself be prime. Since \(p\) is prime, there are exactly two relevant possibilities:
\[
p\mid v \qquad\text{or}\qquad \gcd(p,v)=1. \tag{2}
\]
The second alternative follows from \(p\nmid v\), because a prime is coprime to every number it does not divide.

Also, \(m=2n+1\) is odd. Hence every prime divisor of \(m\), in particular \(p\), is odd. Moreover, because \(m=pv\) is odd, \(v\) is odd as well.

We deal separately with the two alternatives in (2).

### Case 1: \(p\mid v\)

In this case we will derive a contradiction directly from the absolute Euler property, without needing to choose a putative solution \(b\).

First we show that every prime divisor of \(m\) divides \(v\). Let \(r\) be a prime with \(r\mid m=pv\). By Euclid's lemma, \(r\mid p\) or \(r\mid v\). If \(r\mid p\), then, since both \(r\) and \(p\) are prime, \(r=p\); the assumption \(p\mid v\) then again gives \(r\mid v\). Thus
\[
r\text{ prime and }r\mid m\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r\mid v. \tag{3}
\]
It follows that
\[
\gcd(1+v,m)=1. \tag{4}
\]
For if this gcd were greater than \(1\), it would have a prime divisor \(r\). Then \(r\mid m\), so (3) would give \(r\mid v\); but also \(r\mid1+v\). Therefore \(r\mid(1+v)-v=1\), impossible for a prime.

Next, the residue of \(v\) modulo \(m\) is square-zero. Indeed, write \(v=pd\), using \(p\mid v\). Then
\[
v^2=v(pd)=(pv)d=md,
\]
so
\[
v^2\equiv0\pmod m. \tag{5}
\]
It follows that all terms of degree at least two vanish in the binomial expansion of \((1+v)^n\), and hence
\[
(1+v)^n\equiv1+nv\pmod m. \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, this identity can also be proved inductively: if \((1+v)^k\equiv1+kv\), then, using \(v^2\equiv0\),
\[
(1+v)^{k+1}\equiv(1+kv)(1+v)
 =1+(k+1)v+kv^2
 \equiv1+(k+1)v\pmod m.
\]

By (4), the integer \(1+v\) is coprime to \(m\), so (1) says that
\[
(1+v)^n\equiv1\pmod m
\quad\text{or}\quad
(1+v)^n\equiv-1\pmod m. \tag{7}
\]
The second possibility is impossible. Indeed, reducing modulo \(p\), we have \(v\equiv0\pmod p\), and therefore
\[
(1+v)^n\equiv1^n=1\pmod p.
\]
If it were also congruent to \(-1\) modulo \(m\), it would be congruent to \(-1\) modulo the divisor \(p\). Thus \(1\equiv-1\pmod p\), so \(p\mid2\). Since \(p\) is an odd prime, this is impossible.

Therefore the first possibility in (7) must hold. Combining it with (6) gives
\[
1+nv\equiv1\pmod m,
\]
so
\[
m\mid nv.
\]
As \(m=pv\) and \(v>0\), this says \(pv\mid nv\), and cancellation of the positive factor \(v\) yields
\[
p\mid n. \tag{8}
\]
But \(p\mid m=2n+1\), while (8) implies \(p\mid2n\). Hence \(p\) divides
\[
(2n+1)-2n=1,
\]
which is impossible for a prime. This contradiction eliminates the case \(p\mid v\).

### Case 2: \(\gcd(p,v)=1\)

Assume, toward a contradiction, that there is a base \(b\) with
\[
1\le b<m,
\qquad
b^n\equiv-1\pmod m. \tag{9}
\]
Since both \(p\) and \(v\) divide \(m=pv\), reducing (9) modulo the two factors gives
\[
b^n\equiv-1\pmod p,
\qquad
b^n\equiv-1\pmod v. \tag{10}
\]
In particular, the residue of \(b\) modulo \(v\) is a unit. To see this directly, note first that \(n\ge1\), since \(m=2n+1>1\). From the second congruence in (10),
\[
b\bigl(-b^{n-1}\bigr)=-b^n\equiv1\pmod v.
\]
Thus \(-b^{n-1}\) is an inverse of \(b\) modulo \(v\).

Because \(p\) and \(v\) are coprime, the Chinese remainder theorem gives a residue class \(x\pmod m\) uniquely determined by
\[
x\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad
x\equiv b\pmod v. \tag{11}
\]
This residue class is a unit modulo \(m\): its component modulo \(p\) is \(1\), a unit, and its component modulo \(v\) is \(b\), which was just shown to be a unit. Equivalently, the standard representative of \(x\) is coprime to \(m\), so the absolute Euler condition (1) applies to it.

Taking \(n\)-th powers in (11) and using (10), we obtain
\[
x^n\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad
x^n\equiv-1\pmod v. \tag{12}
\]
Thus, under the Chinese remainder identification
\[
\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\cong
\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z/v\mathbb Z,
\]
the element \(x^n\) corresponds to the pair
\[
(1,-1). \tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, (1) says that \(x^n\) must be either \(1\) or \(-1\) modulo \(m\). We consider these two possibilities.

If \(x^n\equiv1\pmod m\), then its CRT components must be \((1,1)\). Comparing this with (13) gives
\[
-1\equiv1\pmod v,
\]
so \(v\mid2\). But \(v>1\) and \(v\) is odd. No such integer can divide \(2\), a contradiction.

If \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod m\), then its CRT components must be \((-1,-1)\). Comparing this with (13) gives
\[
1\equiv-1\pmod p,
\]
so \(p\mid2\). This is impossible because \(p\) is odd.

Both alternatives required by the absolute Euler property are therefore impossible. Hence no \(b\) satisfying (9) exists in the coprime-factor case either.

The two cases in (2) exhaust all possibilities. We conclude that there is no integer \(b\) with \(1\le b<m=2n+1\) for which
\[
b^n\equiv-1\pmod{2n+1}.
\]
Therefore the set counted by \(a(n)\) is empty, and consequently
\[
\boxed{a(n)=0}.
\]
